01.r: The article turns the following phrase into a description of a person: the one who had received.

02.r: Sets the third servant apart from the others.

03.r: Points back to the single talent already mentioned.

04.r: The one talent, the smallest share.
04.n: Greek says only 'the one'; the talent is understood. The BSB writes 'the one talent'.

05.r: The talent given to him by his master.
05.n: An aorist participle, simply 'having received'. Later in the parable, where this servant comes to give his account, the same verb is a perfect participle: received and still held.

06.r: He goes off by himself with the talent.
06.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having gone away', joined to 'dug'.

07.r: He digs a hole to bury the money.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to dig' and cites this verse for its use with 'ground' as the object.

10.n: In our text 'ground' is the direct object, without an article: 'he dug ground'. The Textus Receptus reads 'in the ground' instead.

11.r: Joins the hiding to the digging.

12.r: He puts the money out of sight in the hole.
12.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to hide, conceal' and cites this verse. The Textus Receptus has a compound form, 'hid away'.

13.r: The article; English uses 'his master's' instead.

14.r: The master's money, thought of as silver.
14.n: Abbott-Smith gives the proper sense as 'a piece of silver' and files this verse under 'money'. This study keeps 'silver' to keep the word apart from the other money terms in the parable, such as 'talent'.

15.r: The article with master; English uses 'his' instead.

16.r: The man who owns him and the money.
16.n: A human owner, so 'master' by this study's register. STEPBible tags this occurrence with the human sense.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads ἐν τῇ γῇ, 'in the ground', where our text has the bare object 'ground', which gives the KJV's 'digged in the earth'. It also has ἀπέκρυψεν, 'hid away', for ἔκρυψεν, 'hid'; the KJV's 'hid' does not show the difference.
